What the book’s rules say

Illustrative example from the book: Meridian Industries

Closest archetype: Meridian Industries

30-month plan with three core waves; the hardest version, so it shows every mechanism.

Starting point in the book: Two legacy ERPs, a mainframe, cloud suites and 620 interfaces (USD 5.0B manufacturer).

Why: several legacy ERPs; a mainframe running core logic; hundreds of interfaces; large revenue; manufacturing.

Book, Ch 26.1.3 Book, Ch 01.7.4

Outcomes first

An outcome is a measurable change in a business result, not an agent. Value each one with its formula.

  • Capacity (cost): hours saved x loaded rate x capture factor. Typical mistake: Capture factor = 1.
  • Leakage avoided: spend in scope x leakage rate x recovery rate. Typical mistake: Counting one-time recovery as recurring.
  • Working capital: days reduced x daily balance. Typical mistake: Booking cash release as profit.

Book, Ch 21.2.1 Book, Ch 21.2.2

Two clocks

You have a core clock and an autonomy clock.

  • Core clock: waves of 6-12 months, set by migration, testing, cutover rehearsals and support dates. It speeds up only a little, at high risk.
  • Autonomy clock: promotions of 1-3 months, set by evidence. It speeds up only by collecting evidence faster.
  • Rule: sequence agents behind the waves, not in parallel with them. Agents on cloud suites already in their target state can start early.

Legacy ERP (2)

  1. Does support end before your earliest safe finish (plan plus 25% contingency)? Yes
  2. Does the vendor standard fit 80% or more of the scope? Yes
  3. Are several legacy cores merging into one? Yes
  4. Is converted history needed in the new core, after the two-year history rule? No
  5. Are there small entities with simple needs? Yes

Strategies that apply: Greenfield implementation + Two-tier + Composable / clean core.

Support ends before your safe finish; several cores merge, and greenfield consolidation is usually cheaper than converting each; small entities with simple needs take a lighter tier-2 ERP. Clean core combines with any path. Book, Ch 11.5.1

Mainframe

  1. Hardware or skills risk within 24 months? No
  2. Does the new ERP cover its logic in standard? No
  3. Is it differentiating logic with stable rules? Yes

Strategies that apply: Wrap first, always + Refactor or rebuild behind the same API.

Differentiating logic with stable rules. Book, Ch 11.12.2

Two human gates come before any build: the steering committee approves the strategy per core, then the wave plan.

Book, Ch 26.1.1 Book, Ch 11.4.1 Book, Ch 11.5.2

Foundations first

Invest now in data readiness. Bigger budgets above it wait for its evidence.

  1. 1 Data readiness Gates investment now
    2 of 5 evidenced. Missing: source authority, lineage, ownership.
  2. 2 Platform stress test Waits for the layer below
    2 of 6 evidenced. Missing: load, latency, observability, cost.
  3. 3 Govern the agentic layer Waits for the layer below
    0 of 4 evidenced. Missing: what agents may do, when humans step in, tracing and reversal, ownership.
  4. 4 Agents Waits for the layers below

Rule: before a layer gets a bigger budget, show evidence that the layer beneath it is ready. No agent pilot that depends on a data product starts until that product passes its quality gate.

Starting stage: 1. It permits L1 everywhere; L2 in pilots with full review. The weakest dimension sets the stage; here only data and governance are rated, so confirm the rest with evidence. Book, Ch 26.13.3

Book, Ch 26.2.1 Book, Ch 26.2.2

Engine routing for your value streams

For each decision, use the simplest engine that can do the work:

  1. Stable logic you can write down: rule or workflow.
  2. A prediction on tabular data: model.
  3. An optimization with clear constraints: solver.
  4. Investigation across sources, judgment on unstructured content and an action in a system: agent.

Phases and gates

30 months to G3, then 3 months of handover. Earliest safe finish with 25% contingency: about month 38 (Ch 11.3.2).

  1. Phase 0 Mobilize Months 1-3; exit gate G0
  2. Phase 1 Foundation and pilots Months 4-13; exit gate G1
  3. Phase 2 First go-live Months 14-19; exit gate G2
  4. Phase 3 Scale Months 20-30; exit gate G3
  5. Phase 4 Run Months 31-33; exit gate G4

A gate is a decision, not a meeting: go, go with dated conditions, or stop. It passes when every value signal is at or above plan and no risk counterweight is worse than at the previous gate. Book, Ch 26.3.3 Book, Ch 26.3.5

Book, Ch 26.3.1 Book, Ch 26.3.2 Months are Meridian’s illustrative plan.

Your first 90 days

  1. Write each outcome as one sentence and test it: metric, baseline and target, date, one executive, a guardrail. Book, Ch 21.2.1
  2. Charter, team, signed baselines and architecture decisions. Book, Ch 26.3.1
  3. Run the five questions once per legacy core; the steering committee approves a strategy per core (gate 1). Book, Ch 11.5.2
  4. Check each support deadline against your earliest safe finish: start + duration + 25% contingency. Book, Ch 11.3.2
  5. Fund data readiness first. Show evidence for: source authority, lineage, ownership. Book, Ch 26.2.1
  6. Approve the governance plane design and the do-not-automate list. Book, Ch 26.3.5
  7. Score the risk register: one named executive owner per risk. Book, Ch 26.9.1
  8. Name an agent business owner for each pilot. Book, Ch 24.3.2
  9. Get 3 shadow agents running, each with signed criteria, stop criteria and a disposition date. Book, Ch 26.6.1
  10. End of month 3, gate G0: go, go with dated conditions, or stop. Book, Ch 26.3.3

Book, Ch 26.3.1 Book, Ch 26.3.2

Each pilot runs 8 weeks including a month-end, with criteria signed before the build. Shadow exit needs at least 300 cases, error at or below the human baseline and zero critical errors. Book, Ch 26.6.3 Book, Ch 26.7.1

Give every agent one business owner and a net contribution account from day one: value minus meters, compute, review, incidents and allocated cost. No account, no promotion. Book, Ch 24.3.2 Book, Ch 25.4.12

The start level and ceiling are set by reversibility and impact, not model quality. Appetite never raises a ceiling. Book, Ch 21.4.3 Book, Ch 01.5.4

Top risks your inputs trigger

  • COR-01 Migration larger than estimated. You have a legacy core to move. Book, Ch 26.10.2
  • INT-02 Bridges break intercompany. Several legacy ERPs run side by side during the waves. Book, Ch 26.10.3
  • DAT-01 Master data duplicates. Source authority or ownership is not yet evidenced. Book, Ch 26.10.4
  • CTL-01 Rubber-stamp approvals. Every pilot starts with people approving agent proposals. Book, Ch 26.10.6
  • STR-02 Freed capacity absorbed. You chose capacity as an outcome. Book, Ch 26.10.1
  • PPL-01 Fear and bypass. Agents take over tasks people do today. Book, Ch 26.10.7
  • VND-03 Metering and price changes. Several cloud suites each ship a meter. Book, Ch 26.10.8
  • INT-04 Mainframe wrap late. Agents depend on APIs in front of the mainframe. Book, Ch 26.10.3

Also triggered: VND-01 Capability not GA; INT-01 Hidden interfaces found late; COR-02 Migration starves agent work of key users; DAT-04 Traces not retained or queryable; CTL-06 Kill switch without staffed fallback; CTL-02 Conflicting duties across platforms; DAT-03 Definitions differ across entities.

Write each as cause, event and effect, with one named executive owner, a key risk indicator and dated mitigations. No gate passes with a red risk that has no dated mitigation.
